title: America delivers stinging rebuke to Trump: Democrats sweep Congress
where: Front page (Reuters; C Raja Mohan; Shubhajit Roy), Explained page 12 (Shubhajit Roy; Ravi Dutta Mishra) and editorial, page 10
syllabus: GS2 › Comparison of the Indian constitutional scheme with that of other countries (separation of powers, checks and balances) · GS2 › Effect of policies and politics of developed countries on India's interests; India–US relations; Indian diaspora · GS4 › Accountability in public life
summary: Democrats won control of both the US Senate (at least 54–44) and the House in the midterms, a rebuke to President Trump driven by the cost of living, the Iran war and corruption; Delhi is 'cautiously optimistic'.
ideas: Democracy corrects itself: voters chose issues (soaring fuel prices, an intractable Iran war, perceived corruption) over identity, and handed a check to a President who had assumed extra-large powers.
GS2 · Comparative polity / accountability
The 2026 US midterms show the ballot box restoring checks and balances when the executive outgrows its limits.
Checks built into the presidential model: the House can impeach and the Senate tries; the Senate confirms appointments and approves treaties by a two-thirds majority; the President can veto bills.
GS2 · Separation of powers (India vs USA)
In the US, a hostile Congress checks the President through funding, confirmations, treaties and impeachment, not through a no-confidence vote.

Limits of those checks: Trump has issued 166 executive orders in two years and used a national-interest waiver to nullify Russia sanctions passed with veto-proof majorities, so expect 'rule by executive decree'.
GS2 · Executive power
Executive orders and waivers show how a determined President can bypass even a Congress controlled by the opposition.
Foreign policy has domestic costs: the US–Israel war on Iran raised fuel prices and tariffs acted as a tax on Americans; Vice President Vance said 'the reason we lost is the war'.
GS2 · Effect of policies of developed countries
The midterms show that wars and tariffs abroad are paid for by voters at home, and voters punish them.

For India: wrap up the long-pending trade deal and cooperation in energy, defence and technology now, but engage 'the many Americas' (Congress, business, campuses, think tanks, diaspora) as in the 1990s–2000s; expect closer scrutiny of human rights.
GS2 · India–US relations / Diaspora
India must build bipartisan friends across Congress, business and the diaspora, as it did for the 2008 nuclear deal, not bet on one President.
keywords: Lame duck
An office-holder with limited time and weakened power, often freer to act abroad
GS2 · Executive power
A lame-duck President hemmed in at home often turns to foreign policy, as Delhi now expects of Trump.
Divided government
When the presidency and Congress are controlled by different parties
GS2 · Comparative polity
Divided government is the presidential system's built-in check, possible because the executive does not sit in the legislature.
War Powers Resolution
A US Congress measure directing the President to end hostilities without its approval
GS2 · Separation of powers
Congress passed a War Powers Resolution on Iran in June 2026, yet the war went on, showing the limits of legislative checks.
Section 301 investigation
US trade law route to impose tariffs on 'unfair' practices such as overcapacity
GS2 · India–US trade
The USTR's Section 301 overcapacity probe can reset tariffs on India whatever Congress thinks.
Rule by executive decree
Governing through executive orders instead of legislation
GS2 · Executive power
Rule by executive decree weakens deliberation, which is why parliamentary checks on ordinances matter in India too.
data: Issued by Trump in his second term, against 162 by Biden in a full term, 42 by Bush and 35 by Obama
Mohan Kumar, former Indian ambassador (in IE Explained)
Trump issued 166 executive orders in two years, more than Biden's 162 in a full term, a sign of rule by decree.
examples: India–US civil nuclear agreement, 2008
Won through bipartisan support in Congress, not just leader-to-leader deals
GS2 · India–US relations
The 2008 nuclear deal shows that lasting India–US gains need bipartisan backing in Congress, not just presidential goodwill.
'The reason we lost is the war'
Vice President Vance blames the Iran war for the defeat
GS2 · Foreign policy and domestic politics
Vance's admission that the Iran war cost the Senate shows how foreign wars become domestic liabilities.
Legislatures that resemble society
First Muslim senator; Georgia, Florida and Wisconsin elect their first Black governors; first Latino governors in Texas and California; first Native American governor in New Mexico
GS4
GS2 · Representative democracy · GS4 · Inclusion
In 2026 American voters made their legislatures look more like their society: representative democracy at its best.
pyqs: Separation of powers in India vs the US presidential model; PM vs US President.
Pardon power of the President in India and the USA; limits; preemptive pardons.
India and the USA: basic tenets of the two political systems.
Indian Constitution: checks and balances rather than strict separation of powers.
Friction in India–US ties: Washington yet to find India a place in its global strategy.
Indian diaspora's role in the politics and economy of America and Europe.

trend.t: Comparative questions on India and the USA have moved from broad tenets of the two systems (2018) to one institution or value at a time: equality (2021), secularism (2024), the pardon power (2025) and separation of powers with PM vs President (2026). India–US relations questions shifted from friction over India's place in US strategy (2019) to defence deals and the diaspora's political role (2020).
trend.watch: An India–USA comparison has been asked in 2018, 2021, 2024, 2025 and 2026, so it is a must-study topic. Each question picks one power or institution and asks how it works in both countries, so know the US checks (veto, impeachment, Senate confirmation, treaties) precisely.
focus: Separation of powers and checks on the executive in both systems
Specific powers: veto, pardon, impeachment, executive orders vs ordinances
India–US partnership beyond leaders: Congress, business, diaspora
Effect of US domestic politics (tariffs, visas, wars) on India

potential: Compare the mechanisms that check executive power in the presidential system of the USA and the parliamentary system of India. Which is more effective? (15 marks)
"India must engage the many Americas, not just the White House." In the light of the 2026 US midterm elections, discuss the changing nature of India–US relations. (15 marks)
How do US policies on tariffs and H-1B visas affect India's interests? What should India's response be? (10 marks)

practice.q: Compare the mechanisms that check executive power in the presidential system of the USA and the parliamentary system of India. Which is more effective?
parts: Checks in the US presidential system
Checks in the Indian parliamentary system

answer.t: In November 2026 American voters handed both houses of Congress to the opposition Democrats, placing 'guardrails' on President Trump; India checks its executive through a different, fused design.

answer.h: Checks in the US presidential system

pts.t: The President is elected separately and is not a member of Congress, so the legislature can be controlled by a rival party (divided government).
pts.ex: Democrats control the Senate (at least 54–44) and the House from January 2027.

pts.t: Congress controls funding, so it can cut money for policies or wars it opposes.
pts.ex: Democrats may try to stop funding for the Iran war.

pts.t: The Senate confirms Cabinet members, federal judges and other appointments and approves treaties by a two-thirds majority.
pts.ex: A Democratic Senate can block Supreme Court nominees.

pts.t: The House can impeach the President and the Senate conducts the trial.
pts.ex: Lawmakers may seek the impeachment of Defense Secretary Hegseth.

pts.t: Courts can strike down executive action that exceeds the law.
pts.ex: Some of Trump's tariffs were ruled an illegal tax by US courts.

pts.t: Midterms every two years act as a referendum; the Constitution bars a third term.
pts.ex: The 2026 midterms as a 'referendum' on Trump.

answer.h: Checks in the Indian parliamentary system

pts.t: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)) and must resign if it loses a no-confidence motion.
pts.ex: The fall of the Vajpayee government by one vote in 1999.

pts.t: Question Hour, debates and motions make ministers answer in Parliament every sitting day.
pts.ex: Zero Hour and calling-attention motions.

pts.t: Parliamentary committees and the CAG examine spending and policy in detail.
pts.ex: The Public Accounts Committee examines CAG audit reports.

pts.t: Courts can strike down laws and executive acts, and even constitutional amendments that violate the basic structure.
pts.ex: Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

pts.t: An ordinance lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless approved (Article 123).
pts.ex: Re-promulgation of ordinances held a fraud on the Constitution (Krishna Kumar Singh, 2017).

pts.t: States and a Rajya Sabha without a ruling majority can slow the Union executive.
pts.ex: Bills held up in the Rajya Sabha before the ruling party gained a majority.

pts.t: Because the executive and legislature are separate, a rival Congress can block laws, appointments and funds outright.
pts.ex: Trump's 'VETO' cap shows a stand-off of equals.

pts.k: But US checks invite gridlock and bypass
pts.t: A blocked President governs by executive order and waivers, and gridlock can stall the budget itself.
pts.ex: 166 executive orders in two years; waiver used to nullify Russia sanctions.

pts.t: A government faces Parliament every day and can fall at any time, not only at fixed elections.

pts.k: But Indian checks weaken with a strong majority
pts.t: Fusion of executive and legislature, the anti-defection law and whips let a majority government dominate the House.
pts.ex: The Tenth Schedule binds MPs to the party line.

pts.t: Fewer sittings and less committee scrutiny of bills dilute oversight.
Refer more bills to department-related standing committees as a rule.
Guarantee enough sitting days for real scrutiny.
Limit whips to confidence and money votes so MPs can scrutinise freely.
Give the Opposition more space through a shadow-cabinet style system and chairs of key committees.
Use ordinances only in genuine urgency, as courts have warned.
Borrow US-style confirmation hearings for key regulators without importing gridlock.

answer.t: The US system checks power by dividing it, India by making it answerable every day; neither works without an alert electorate, as the 2026 midterms show.

title: Energy security after the Hormuz shock: Iran exempts Indian ships; LPG imports from West Asia recover
where: Nation, page 9 (PTI); Economy, page 13 (Sukalp Sharma); Politics, page 7 (Reuters, US sanctions)
syllabus: GS2 › Effect of policies and politics of other countries on India's interests (West Asia, US sanctions); India's bilateral relations (Iran) · GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; energy security
summary: Iran has exempted ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar from Strait of Hormuz transit restrictions, and India's LPG imports from the Gulf have recovered through ship-to-ship transfers, even as the US sanctioned India-based entities for aiding Iran.
evolution: For energy security, E100 alone is not the answer.
Energy security depends on if we electrify, and how.
Indian Navy frees the hijacked vessel Azini off Somalia; attacks on shipping during the West Asia war.
ideas: Diplomacy keeps the strait open: Iran exempted Indian ships from Hormuz restrictions on 'mutual interests', saying the aim was to allow imports of medicines, while China's exemption was meant to secure its political support.
GS2 · India–Iran / West Asia
Iran's Hormuz exemption for Indian ships shows that steady ties with every side are India's best insurance at chokepoints.

Supply recovers through risk-taking logistics: Gulf suppliers are using ship-to-ship transfers to move LPG through Hormuz; imports from the UAE rose 240% and from Kuwait 248% in September–October over March–August (Kpler).
GS3 · Energy security
Ship-to-ship transfers restored Gulf LPG flows, but they are a stopgap that adds risk and cost.

Diversification as a shock absorber: US LPG imports rose sharply during the disruption and fell 36% as Gulf flows improved; overall imports remain below pre-war levels due to lower demand and higher domestic production.
GS3 · Energy security
During the Hormuz crisis US LPG acted as India's swing supply: diversified sources absorb shocks.

Caught in great-power crossfire: under 'Operation Economic Outcast', the US sanctioned India-based individuals and entities for providing false flags and certifications to sanctioned tankers carrying Iranian oil.
GS2 · Effect of US policies on India
US secondary sanctions on India-based firms show how great-power conflicts reach into India's shipping and business.
Strategic autonomy under strain: India must keep Iran's goodwill for safe passage while managing US pressure, showing that energy security is a core driver of its West Asia policy.
GS2 · Strategic autonomy
Balancing Iran's goodwill and US pressure is strategic autonomy in practice, with energy security as the stake.
keywords: Ship-to-ship (STS) transfer
Moving cargo between vessels at sea to reroute or reduce exposure
GS3 · Energy logistics
STS transfers kept LPG moving through Hormuz, but such workarounds raise insurance and safety risks.
Chokepoint
A narrow sea passage whose closure disrupts global trade
GS1 · Straits / GS3 · Energy security
Hormuz is the chokepoint where India's energy security is most exposed.
Secondary sanctions
Penalties on third-country firms that deal with a sanctioned state
GS2 · Effect of US policies

False flagging
Registering tankers under misleading flags to hide sanctioned cargo
GS3 · Maritime security
False flagging of tankers shows how 'shadow fleets' undermine maritime governance.
Swing supplier
A source that can raise or cut output quickly to balance a market
GS3 · Energy security
US LPG served as India's swing supplier when Gulf flows collapsed.

trend.t: Questions began with geography and resources (oil distribution, 2021; straits, 2022) and West Asian energy cooperation (2017), widened to the effect of US–Iran tensions on India (2018), and now treat energy security as central to foreign policy (GS2, 2025) and to growth with sustainability (GS3, 2026).
trend.watch: Energy security was asked in GS2 in 2025 and GS3 in 2026, so it is a must-study area. Questions link energy with foreign policy: expect West Asia, chokepoints and sanctions to recur.
focus: Energy diplomacy with West Asia and Iran
Chokepoints and maritime security of energy routes
US sanctions and India's strategic autonomy

practice.q: How do disruptions at maritime chokepoints threaten India's energy security? Suggest a strategy to make India's energy supplies resilient.

answer.t: Since the West Asia war began in February 2026, energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz plummeted, forcing India to rely on Iranian exemptions, ship-to-ship transfers and US supplies.

pts.t: India imports most of its crude oil and much of its LPG and LNG, largely from the Gulf.
pts.ex: UAE, Qatar and Kuwait were the top LPG sources before the war.

pts.t: Disruptions raise global prices, feeding inflation and widening the current account deficit.
pts.ex: War-driven fuel prices hit economies worldwide.

pts.t: LPG shortages hit clean cooking for millions of households.
pts.ex: PM Ujjwala Yojana beneficiaries.

pts.t: Attacks on shipping endanger Indian crews and cargo.
pts.ex: Attacks on vessels in West Asia (2026).

pts.t: War-risk premiums and longer routes raise costs.
pts.ex: Ship-to-ship transfers add risk.

pts.t: Securing supply from one side can invite sanctions from another.
pts.ex: US sanctions on India-based entities aiding Iran.

pts.t: Spread imports across regions so one chokepoint cannot cut supply.
pts.ex: US LPG filled the gap during the disruption.

pts.t: Expand strategic petroleum reserves and add LPG and gas storage.
pts.ex: SPRs at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur.

pts.t: Keep working ties with all Gulf states and Iran for safe passage.
pts.ex: Iran's Hormuz exemption for Indian ships.

pts.t: Escort and protect shipping in key sea lanes.
pts.ex: Navy deployments and the Azini rescue (Nov 2026).

pts.t: Develop corridors and ports that bypass single chokepoints.
pts.ex: IMEC; Chabahar.

pts.t: Renewables, storage, electrification, biofuels and domestic production.
pts.ex: Ethanol blending; storage VGF scheme (2026).

pts.t: Build an Indian-flagged fleet and insurance capacity.

answer.t: The Hormuz crisis shows that energy security rests on diplomacy, diversity and domestic clean energy together; the cheapest barrel is the one India does not need to import.

title: On Govt agenda: New Rs 2,800-cr capex scheme for critical minerals
where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Pratyush Deep), with an Explained box
syllabus: GS3 › Industrial policy and its effects on industrial growth; Infrastructure: energy; Mobilisation of resources · GS1 › Distribution of key natural resources across the world and India · GS2 › Effect of policies of other countries on India's interests (China) · GS4 › Ethical issues in international relations
summary: The Union Cabinet is likely to take up a scheme of about Rs 2,800 crore that offers a 30% capital subsidy for two lithium and two nickel processing plants, to build India's domestic critical mineral processing base.
evolution: PM sets a 500 GW non-fossil capacity goal; storage needs batteries (energy thread).
Cabinet to consider a capex scheme for lithium and nickel processing.
ideas: The gap is processing, not only mining: India has little processing capacity and is almost fully import-dependent for cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths and silicon.
GS3 · Industry / GS1 · Resources
India's critical mineral weakness lies in processing; mining ore is of little use without the capacity to refine it.
Concentration as a strategic risk: China dominates global critical mineral processing and has used it as leverage in trade tensions, leaving India open to supply disruptions.
GS2 · India–China / GS3 · Economy
China's hold over mineral processing turns supply chains into tools of pressure, so diversification is national security.
Capex support to start a domestic base: a 30% capital subsidy for four plants (two lithium, two nickel) aims to turn ores into high-purity compounds, with cobalt recovered from nickel.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Capital subsidies for processing plants target the costliest, riskiest link in India's mineral value chain.
Clean-energy and strategic sectors depend on it: the minerals feed electric mobility, battery storage, electronics, defence and speciality steel.
GS3 · Energy / Defence industry
Without lithium, nickel and cobalt, India's EV and battery ambitions rest on imported inputs.
Cluster approach: processing parks in four states, each built as an ecosystem for one mineral, backed by a planned stockpile under the National Critical Minerals Mission.
GS1 · Location of industries / GS3 · Industrial policy
Mineral-specific parks link resource geography to industry, and a strategic stockpile insures against shocks.
keywords: Mid-stream processing
Refining ores into high-purity chemicals used by battery and electronics makers
GS3 · Industry
India's critical mineral challenge is mid-stream: refining, not just mining.
Weaponisation of supply chains
Using dominance over a resource to pressure other countries
GS2 · IR / GS3 · Economy
China's control of mineral processing shows how supply chains can be weaponised in trade disputes.
Strategic stockpile
A government reserve held to ride out supply disruptions
GS3 · Economy / Security
A critical mineral stockpile works like a strategic oil reserve for the battery age.
Value-chain localisation
Building each stage of production at home
GS3 · Industrial policy
Localising the mineral value chain cuts import dependence from mine to battery.
Resource-based clusters
Industrial parks placed near the raw material they use
GS1 · Location of industries
Odisha's nickel and Gujarat's heavy rare earths show resource-based clustering in practice.
data: Allocation committed for a National Critical Mineral Stockpile Programme, 2024-25 to 2030-31
National Critical Minerals Mission (Government of India), via IE
The government has committed Rs 500 crore (2024-25 to 2030-31) for a critical mineral stockpile under the NCMM.
examples: Four mineral-specific processing parks
Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh for rare earths, Odisha for nickel, Maharashtra for lithium
GS1 · Distribution of resources · GS3 · Industrial policy
Matching parks to state resources (Odisha's nickel, Gujarat's heavy rare earths) is a model of resource-based industrialisation.
China's leverage over mineral processing
Dominance used as leverage in trade tensions
GS4
GS2 · India–China · GS3 · Economy · GS4 · Ethics in IR
China's use of mineral processing as leverage is a clear example of economic interdependence turned into coercion.
Odisha as a gateway for imported nickel
Eastern location suits imports from Indonesia
GS1 · Location of industries · GS2 · Act East
Odisha's eastern coast lets India process nickel imported from Indonesia, linking resources to the Act East region.
pyqs: The West fostering India as an alternative to China's supply chains.
Challenges for India as the world moves from free trade to protectionism; how to meet them.
Rationale, achievements and improvements of the PLI scheme.

trend.t: Mineral questions began in physical geography (resource distribution, mining's low GDP share, 2017–2022) and industrial location (2019, 2020). From 2024 the frame shifted to supply chains and geopolitics: India as an alternative to China (2024), protectionism and industrial incentives such as PLI (2025).
trend.watch: Supply-chain resilience and China-plus-one questions are rising since 2024, while mining's environmental cost was asked again in 2025. Critical minerals sit where these meet, so expect a direct question soon.
focus: Industrial policy tools: PLI, capex subsidies, parks
Resource geography and location of processing
Environmental cost of mining and processing

potential: "Critical minerals are to the 21st century what oil was to the 20th." Discuss India's vulnerabilities and the steps needed to secure its critical mineral supply chains. (15 marks)
Why has India remained import-dependent for critical minerals despite its resource base? Examine the role of processing capacity. (10 marks)
How can mineral-specific processing parks promote regional industrial development in India? (10 marks)

practice.q: "Critical minerals are to the 21st century what oil was to the 20th." Discuss India's vulnerabilities and the steps needed to secure its critical mineral supply chains.

answer.t: In November 2026 the Union Cabinet is set to consider a Rs 2,800-crore capex scheme for lithium and nickel processing, as India remains almost fully import-dependent for key critical minerals.

pts.t: Lithium, nickel and cobalt are core to Li-ion batteries for EVs and grid storage.
pts.ex: Needed for India's 500 GW non-fossil goal.

pts.t: Smartphones, semiconductors and electronics depend on these minerals.
Defence systems and speciality steels need rare earths and alloys.
Like oil, control of supply gives power over others.
pts.ex: China's processing dominance used in trade tensions.

pts.t: India relies almost completely on imports for cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths and silicon.
Even where ore exists, India lacks refining capacity to make battery-grade compounds.
Global processing is concentrated in China, which has curbed exports of some minerals in the past.
pts.ex: Export curbs on gallium and germanium (2023).

pts.t: Large parts of India's mineral potential remain unexplored.
Processing plants are costly and technology-intensive, deterring private investment.
Mining and chemical processing can damage land, water and local communities.
30% capital subsidy for lithium and nickel plants under the proposed scheme.
pts.ex: Rs 500–900 crore cap per beneficiary.

pts.t: A mission-mode approach to exploration, processing and overseas assets, with a planned stockpile.
pts.ex: Rs 500 crore committed for stockpiling (2024-25 to 2030-31).

pts.t: Ecosystems in four states matched to their resources.
pts.ex: Odisha for nickel, Gujarat and AP for rare earths.

pts.t: Secure supplies abroad through state firms and partners.
pts.ex: KABIL; India's membership of the Minerals Security Partnership.

pts.t: Recover minerals from used batteries and e-waste to reduce fresh demand.
Strict environmental norms and benefit-sharing with mining communities.
pts.ex: District Mineral Foundations.

answer.t: Just as oil security shaped the last century, building domestic processing, diverse partners and a strategic stockpile will decide India's energy and strategic autonomy in this one.

title: An alliance for multilateralism by other means
syllabus: GS2 › Important international institutions, agencies and fora: their structure and mandate; Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India · GS4 › Ethical issues in international relations; Environmental ethics
summary: The Partners for Multilateralism (P4M), launched at the 81st UNGA week and co-sponsored by India among others, commits to strengthening multilateral cooperation; the author argues it needs a concrete plan, clear principles and public engagement to succeed.
evolution: BRICS Parliamentary Forum seeks UNSC reform.
P4M, co-sponsored by India, pledges to strengthen multilateral cooperation.
ideas: Multilateralism under severe pressure: the US, a principal founder and long-time guarantor of the system, is rejecting it in word and deed, and other major players flout rules with impunity.
GS2 · International institutions
With the system's own guarantor walking away, middle and smaller powers must carry multilateralism.
A bridge across divides: co-sponsored by Australia, Brazil, Barbados, Canada, the EU, India and Kenya and signed by 18 more, P4M joins large and small countries of the Global South and North.
GS2 · Groupings involving India
P4M's mixed membership makes it a rare bridge between the Global North and South.

Reform language reflects a power shift: its pledge of cooperation that is 'open, fair, equitable, inclusive' echoes the South's long demand, now heard in a North weakened by Western turmoil and Transatlantic strain.
GS2 · Global order / Global South
The North's new receptiveness to reform reflects the Global South's growing clout and the West's own turmoil.
Plan and principles, or failure: P4M needs an action plan with costs and how they are shared, and clear principles that set it apart from efforts such as China's four Global Initiatives.
GS2 · Effect of policies of other countries
Coalitions without costed plans and clear principles join the list of well-intended but failed initiatives.
Engage people and the planet: reform drives fail when they ignore affected populations; P4M's diversity could offer ideas on deep ecology and interspecies coexistence for a new framework.
GS2 · Global governance / GS4 · Environmental ethics
Multilateralism will regain legitimacy only when it engages the public and protects the planet, not just states.
keywords: Minilateralism / coalition of the willing
Small, flexible groups of like-minded states acting where universal bodies stall
GS2 · Groupings
When universal institutions stall, coalitions of the willing like P4M keep cooperation alive.
Rules-based order
An international system governed by agreed norms rather than power
GS2 · International order
P4M's commitment to institutions and rule of law defends the rules-based order.
Reformed multilateralism
India's call to update global institutions to reflect today's realities
GS2 · India's foreign policy
India's co-sponsorship of P4M fits its long call for reformed multilateralism.
Bridging power
A country able to connect rival blocs
GS2 · India's global role
India's presence in P4M, BRICS and the Quad shows its role as a bridging power.
Deep ecology
A view that nature has value in itself, not only for human use
GS4 · Environmental ethics
Deep ecology asks global institutions to protect the planet for its own sake.

trend.t: Questions moved from the mandates of specific bodies (WTO, Bretton Woods, UNESCO, 2013–2019) to the crisis of the system itself: WTO reform amid trade war (2018), unresolved UN reform and great-power rivalry (2025), the retreat from multilateralism (2025) and BRICS as a voice of the Global South (2026).
trend.watch: Since 2025 UPSC asks about the crisis of multilateralism almost every year. Prepare why the order is weakening, who is reshaping it and India's role as a bridge for the Global South.
focus: Crisis of multilateralism and great-power retreat
Reform of the UN, WTO and other institutions

potential: "Multilateralism is under severe pressure, yet new coalitions are emerging to rescue it." Discuss with reference to India's role. (15 marks)
What are the limits of coalitions of the willing in reforming global governance? (10 marks)
"In international relations, the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must." How can a rules-based order change this? (10 marks, GS4)

practice.q: "Multilateralism is under severe pressure, yet new coalitions are emerging to rescue it." Discuss with reference to India's role.

answer.t: In September 2026, India, the EU, Brazil, Canada, Kenya, Australia and Barbados co-sponsored the Partners for Multilateralism (P4M) at the 81st UNGA, just as the US, the system's founder, turns away from it.

pts.t: The US rejects institutions it built, in word and deed.
pts.ex: Withdrawals from the WHO and the Paris Agreement.

pts.t: Rules are flouted with frequency and impunity.
pts.ex: Wars in Europe and West Asia.

pts.t: Key bodies cannot act or reform.
pts.ex: WTO Appellate Body non-functional since 2019; UNSC reform stalled.

pts.t: Institutions reflect 1945, not today's balance of power.
Competing models of global governance divide states.
pts.ex: China's four Global Initiatives.

pts.t: Institutions seem distant from the people they affect.
Mixed membership builds trust across old divides.
pts.ex: P4M joins large and small states of both.

pts.t: Commitment to cooperation that is open, fair, equitable and inclusive.
Small coalitions act faster than universal bodies.
Groupings amplify developing countries' demands.
pts.ex: BRICS; India's Voice of the Global South summits.

pts.t: Declarations without costed plans fade.
Without clarity, they overlap with rival initiatives.
Ignoring affected people breeds discontent.
Many small coalitions can weaken universal institutions.
India sits in the Quad, BRICS, SCO and P4M and can link rival blocs.
Push the South's agenda on finance, climate and technology.
pts.ex: African Union's G20 membership under India's 2023 presidency.

pts.t: Press for UNSC and WTO reform with like-minded partners.
pts.ex: G4 for UNSC reform.

pts.t: Back P4M with concrete projects, costs and burden-sharing.
Bring civilisational ideas such as Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam and LiFE into global norms.
pts.ex: G20 theme 'One Earth, One Family, One Future'.

pts.t: Keep commitments, as on climate targets met early.
pts.ex: Paris capacity target met in 2025.

answer.t: As great powers retreat, coalitions like P4M can keep multilateralism alive; India, as a bridging power, can help turn declarations into a fairer, workable order.
